issues.legal_issue: A private landlord’s land does not cease to receive thika-tenant protection merely because a betterment fee was levied on it for an improvement scheme.
material_facts: The tenants were thika tenants, and the landlord brought ejectment suits in the ordinary civil court rather than before the Controller.
The land lay within the area of an improvement scheme and was listed for a possible betterment fee, but it was not acquired for the scheme.
The Board levied a betterment fee on the land because the scheme increased its value, and the landlord accepted the assessment.
The fee contributed to the Board’s funds, which could be used for the general purposes of carrying out improvement schemes.
issues.conclusion: The land was not exempt from the Thika Tenancy Act under section 30(c), because it was not itself required for carrying out a provision of the Improvement Act. The ejectment suits therefore fell within the Act’s ordinary procedure, under which an application for ejectment had to be made to the Controller; the ordinary-court suits were incompetent.
issues.legal_principle: Statutory words must be construed in context, having regard to the statute’s object and policy. Because the Thika Tenancy Act was protective legislation, its exception in section 30(c) had to be strictly construed. The land itself must be directly required for carrying out a specific provision of the Calcutta Improvement Trust Act, 1911; an indirect connection through a fee that augments the Board’s general funds is insufficient. Section 78A concerns land not required for execution of the scheme, and section 122’s use of betterment-fee receipts does not make the land itself necessary for that provision. Sections 30(a) and (b) concern government land and land vested in or possessed by specified bodies, and do not justify extending the exception to a private landlord’s land. Section 5 assigns thika-tenant ejectment applications to the Controller. The Court discussed R. H. Galloway v. The Mayor and Commonality of London and Trustees for the Improvement of Calcutta v. Chandra Kanta Ghosh, but distinguished the broader powers to acquire or deal with land in those contexts from the direct land requirement imposed by section 30(c).

predicates.ejectment_claim_against_protected_tenant: A landlord brings an ejectment claim against a tenant who belongs to a class protected by a special tenancy regime.
predicates.private_landlord_owns_land: The land is owned by a private landlord rather than being land of government or a specified public body.
predicates.land_is_not_itself_needed_for_improvemen: The land itself is not needed to carry out the physical or other specific work required by an improvement scheme.
predicates.only_indirect_connection_is_betterment_f: The land’s connection to the improvement scheme is that a fee was levied on it and the resulting funds may support the scheme generally.

issues.definition: When a private landlord seeks to eject a protected tenant and the land is not itself needed for improvement work but is connected to the scheme only through a betterment fee, the land remains subject to tenant protection.

issues.legal_issue: An exception covering land required for improvement work is not redundant merely because acquired land may already fall within an exception for land vested in a public authority.
material_facts: The landlord argued that if the improvement body were a local authority, land acquired by it would already be covered by the exception for land vested in a local authority, leaving the separate improvement-work exception redundant.
The Court assumed for the purpose of addressing that argument, without deciding, that the improvement body was a local authority.

The Court noted that land not acquired by the Board might nevertheless be needed for improvement work, including work involving the raising, lowering, or levelling of land or the formation or retention of open spaces.
The Court also observed that the legislature may include a provision out of abundant caution.
issues.conclusion: The separate exception was not redundant: it could apply to land that had not been acquired but was nevertheless required for improvement work. The Court did not decide whether the Board was a local authority.
issues.legal_principle: A statutory provision is not necessarily redundant because some of its potential coverage overlaps another provision. The Court read the separate exception as capable of covering land needed for improvement work without being acquired, and noted that the legislature may legislate out of abundant caution. The Court referred to sections 30(b)(iv) and 30(c) of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, and sections 42 and 35C of the Calcutta Improvement Trust Act, 1911.

predicates.thika_tenancy_exemption_case: A court is construing an exception to a special tenancy-protection regime for land required for improvement work.
predicates.some_unacquired_land_may_be_needed_for_i: Improvement work may require land that is not acquired by the improvement body.

issues.definition: When an exception to a tenancy-protection regime concerns land required for improvement work and such work may need unacquired land, the exception has scope independent of an exception for land vested in a public body.
